## What it does

There's a well-worn idea in the ecosystem of sonifying quantum state evolution — mapping amplitudes and phases to pitch, timbre, rhythm. `qiskit-eigenlight` takes the same underlying object — a Hamiltonian's eigenspectrum, probed by continuous-time evolution — and asks what it looks like instead of what it sounds like: rendered as an emission spectrum, with spectral lines positioned at true eigenvalue gaps and colored/intensity-scaled from the actual coherence structure of the evolving state. It is not a music-to-image converter — there's no audio anywhere in this package, just the other rendering of the same physics.

Given a Hamiltonian (real symmetric — e.g. a graph's adjacency matrix) and an initial state, it diagonalizes, evolves under the free Hamiltonian, and decomposes a probe observable's dynamics into its Fourier components: each one sits at a frequency equal to a true energy gap, with amplitude set by the actual coherence between eigenstates. That's the real linear-response decomposition of an observable's dynamics, not a stylized approximation of one.

It also drives **continuous-time quantum walks (CTQW)** directly: build the adjacency matrix of a Cayley graph and get both the walk's mixing/return-probability dynamics and its emission spectrum from the same machinery, with girth and spectral gap computed exactly rather than estimated.

## Stated limitations

The one deliberate simplification: the probe operator defaults to uniform all-pairs coupling rather than a real atom's physical transition operator — a real limitation if you're trying to reproduce an actual physical spectrum, documented rather than buried. Everything is unitary — no dissipation, so spectral lines are infinitely sharp. Adjacency construction currently covers cyclic groups only; products of cyclic groups are an open item, not silently assumed to work.
